videoTitle: The Truth About South Africa’s Economy: Why We Need a Zero-Based Reset
videoDescription: What's actually wrong with how South Africa plans its future? I think the answer is zero-based nation planning, and in this video, I break down exactly what that means and why it matters. Right now, the numbers are brutal: 0.7% average economic growth over the past decade, 1 million young people entering the labor force every year, 46% youth unemployment. At our current capacity, we simply can't move the needle with this approach. I walk through four case studies of countries that rebuilt from almost nothing by starting from zero instead of building on top of a broken past: Singapore turning an entire island into a water catchment system after being expelled from Malaysia with no resources, Botswana institutionalizing long-term development plans from independence, Rwanda authoring Vision 2020 while the wounds of the genocide were still open, and South Korea building state-backed conglomerates after being flattened by war. The common thread: none of these nations waited for permission, acknowledgment, or the past to be resolved before they started building the future. National progress often gets stuck in the past, but true growth starts when we stop building on broken policies. I examine four case studies—Singapore, Botswana, Rwanda, and South Korea—where leaders ignored old constraints to prioritize effective nation-building. These countries prove you don't need to wait for permission to start a new trajectory. South Africa's current statistics are stark, with low economic growth and high youth unemployment defining our reality. By applying zero-based planning, we can stop relying on outdated capacity and start designing systems that actually move the needle. This approach forces us to confront why talent leaves and how power structures often stifle the market. Tell me what you think about whether this model would work here. That car is in British showrooms now, from a brand that sold 51,422 cars here last year — more than Tesla. So what did the engineers find? And is it cheap to make, or cheap to own? Those are two very different promises. This video covers what the teardowns actually showed: Nikkei's engineers found far fewer parts than in rival cars, with eight major components combined into a single drive unit on the Atto 3, and parts shared across multiple models. In October 2024, Japan's government trade bureau laid out over 90,000 parts from 16 foreign EVs in a gymnasium near Nagoya for around 70 Japanese parts makers to study. In Detroit, Caresoft Global — run by a former GM chief engineer with 45 years in the industry — tore down the BYD Seagull (sold here as the Dolphin Surf) and called it a huge problem for American carmakers. And Swiss bank UBS ran its own Seal teardown and found a lasting ~25% cost advantage over Western carmakers, concluding it was "the better and much cheaper car" — while still making roughly a 16% gross margin. Then the half that reaches your driveway: the blade battery built into the car's structure, and why that can turn a moderate knock into a write-off. Why the Seal sits in insurance groups up to 50. The integrated drive unit, and what nobody yet knows about replacing one out of warranty. BYD's ~125 UK sites and what that means outside the big cities. Used Seals from around £28,495 against £45,730 new. Plus how BYD started — as a 1995 battery maker in Shenzhen — and the 2003 Japanese study that said China was ten years behind. Covered honestly too: five Euro NCAP stars, a cobalt-free LFP battery, and one of the best warranties on sale — six years/93,750 miles, and a transferable eight-year/155,350-mile battery warranty. If you own a BYD — Seal, Sealion, Atto 3 or Dolphin — what has ownership really been like? videoTitle: LEBO SEKGOBELA | GOD HAD ANOTHER PLAN | WHO IS LEBO AT HOME | MINISTRY OR BUSINESS | I NEVER QUIT
videoDescription: Before millions of people knew the voice behind “Lion of Judah”, Lebo Sekgobela had already lived through years of rejection, disappointment, service and waiting. In this episode of the King David Studio Podcast, David Mashabela sits down with award-winning South African gospel singer and worshipper Lebo Sekgobela for a deeply personal conversation about the journey behind the music, the woman behind the ministry and what it takes to keep believing when success does not arrive when you expect it. Lebo grew up in Gauteng's Vaal area and spent years developing her voice long before becoming a household name. She worked as a backing vocalist with artists including Vicky Vilakazi and William Sejake, while also serving in church and working outside the music industry. She has spoken openly about entering numerous auditions and talent competitions and repeatedly being turned away. But she kept singing. Her solo journey included Ithemba Lami and By His Grace in 2013 before the release of Restored in 2016 changed everything. The album became a multi-platinum success and introduced Lion of Judah to a much wider audience. The song became one of the defining South African gospel recordings of its era and helped establish Lebo as one of the country's leading worship voices. Interestingly, Lion of Judah was not originally written by Lebo. She has explained that she heard Matsetse Matthews, who wrote the song years earlier, perform it at a conference in Durban in 2015. The message spoke to her, and her eventual recording helped carry the song to a new generation of listeners. In this conversation, David explores the years before the breakthrough. What does repeated rejection do to somebody who believes she has been called to sing? How do you maintain faith when the doors you believe should open keep closing? And when success finally arrives, how do you make sure fame does not change the person you were before anybody knew your name? Lebo has previously said one of her prayers during the height of her success was that the attention and acclaim should not change her character. The conversation also looks at the realities behind gospel music: ministry, business, money, musicians, performance, family life and the responsibility that comes with being regarded not simply as an entertainer, but as a spiritual voice by thousands of people. Lebo's career has continued evolving beyond Lion of Judah. Her catalogue includes projects such as Umusa and Hymns and Worship, while her official biography lists numerous gospel awards and nominations over the years. Lebo sekgobela More recently, she expanded into another creative space when she made her acting debut in the Mzansi Bioskop drama Ingozi, playing Zanele. Lebo described acting as a dream come true and indicated that she was open to exploring more opportunities beyond music. In 2025 she was also building large-scale gospel experiences of her own, including Worshippers Unleashed and Gospel Love and Soul, alongside plans for a nationwide tour and another Hymns and Worship project. But beneath all the achievements remains a remarkable human story: A young woman who was repeatedly told no. A daughter whose family did not have everything. A backing singer waiting for her opportunity. A worshipper who kept serving. And eventually, a voice heard across South Africa and beyond. This is Lebo Sekgobela — beyond “Lion of Judah.” Watch the full conversation with David Mashabela on the King David Studio Podcast. videoDescription: In this powerful and important episode of King David Studio Podcast, David Mashabela sits down with Dr Michael “Mike” Masiapato, Commissioner and CEO of South Africa’s Border Management Authority. South Africa’s borders are at the centre of some of the country’s biggest national conversations: undocumented migration, cross-border crime, human trafficking, smuggling, delays at ports of entry, illegal goods, border corruption, and the balance between national security, lawful trade and human dignity. The BMA was formally established as a Schedule 3A public entity on 1 April 2023, following the Border Management Authority Act of 2020, and was officially launched by President Cyril Ramaphosa on 5 October 2023 in Musina, Limpopo. It was created to bring a more integrated approach to border management after years of fragmented responsibilities across different state departments and agencies. In this conversation, Dr Mike Masiapato explains the work of the BMA, the realities of South Africa’s ports of entry, the difference between border management and border protection, and what it takes to secure a country with complex land, sea and air borders. The discussion goes beyond politics and headlines. It asks the bigger questions: Can South Africa protect its borders without losing its humanity? Can the state fight corruption and organised crime at the border? Can lawful trade and travel be made easier while illegal activity is stopped? And what does a secure border mean for ordinary South Africans? Dr Mike Masiapato brings deep experience from South Africa’s Justice, Crime Prevention and Security Cluster, with a career spanning policing, intelligence, defence intelligence structures and the Financial Intelligence Centre. This is a timely, educational and necessary conversation about sovereignty, safety, trade, migration and the future of South Africa. videoTitle: SABC News Mayoral Debate for the City of Cape Town - Pt1
videoDescription: Neatly ensconced between the mighty blue waters of the Atlantic, and the staggering heights of Table Mountain, but also sprawling out and away in different directions, from these imposing landmarks- lies the City of Cape Town - fondly known as "The Mother City", or Ekapa, in one of this province's official languages - IsiXhosa. It is one of South Africa's 8 metropolitan municipalities, and a formidable player in the national economy - contributing about 10% of national GDP. It is home to nearly 5 million people, with nearly 2 million of those being of voting age, come 4 November. That easily makes the metro - a massive, and much-coverted electoral prize! But it's a prize that's not exchanged hands since 2006 - when the DA's dominance of this city's body-politic began to take shape, when Helen Zille was first elected mayor, replacing the ANC's Nomaindia Mfeketo. Since then, the party has made the city something of a fortress - with a significant gap in percentage support, between the governing party and the opposition. The claim that the City of Cape Town is the best governed city in the country, with superior service delivery, easily rolls off the tongues of its leaders, and the DA broadly. But claims of inequitable development, spatial apartheid, and a sense of one Cape Town - two different city experiences - one for the poor and marginalised, and another for the well-off, are never far from the lips of critics. DA Federal Leader Geordin Hill-Lewis wears the mayoral chain, and has done so since 2021, but each of his fellow-participants in tonight's mayoral debate, will be hoping to be the one to be sworn in - as mayor, a few days after 04 November. videoTitle: Rugare Gumbo — The Man Who Made Mugabe | The Last of the Dare (Full Documentary)
videoDescription: Rugare Gumbo is the last surviving member of Dare reChimurenga, the council that ran ZANU's liberation war. He helped choose Robert Mugabe as the movement's leader, and he spent the rest of his life explaining what that decision cost. Mugabe's government held him in an underground pit in Mozambique for nearly two years. He later served as a minister, defended the party as its spokesman, and was expelled in 2014. At eighty-six he is still writing about the men who run Zimbabwe. This film draws on Gumbo's own interviews, contemporaneous reporting from The Herald and The Guardian, and archive footage. His account of Herbert Chitepo's assassination and of his detention is contested. No one has ever been convicted. It is one life inside ZANU, not the whole history. videoTitle: Acting Justice Tembeka Ngcukaitobi lecture on SA Constitution
videoDescription: Acting Justice Tembeka Ngcukaitobi unpacks South Africa’s Constitution and Bill of Rights in an interactive lecture with learners at the Constitutional Court. He explains who the Constitution protects, the distinction between rights reserved for citizens and those enjoyed by everyone, and what this means for access to education, healthcare and protection from violence. Through practical examples and questions from the students, he explores what the right to basic education should mean in their own classrooms, why rights come with responsibilities, and how ordinary people give meaning to the Constitution. The discussion also tackles discrimination against migrants, gender-based violence, frustrations over service delivery, landmark court judgments and accountability when government fails to comply with court orders. At its heart is Ngcukaitobi’s idea of “constitutionalism from below”: a Constitution that people must actively build, defend and bring to life in their communities. videoTitle: Cutting Edge | Service delivery in the City of Johannesburg
videoDescription: As South Africa heads towards the local government elections, Cutting Edge takes a closer look at the state of service delivery in the City of Johannesburg — and asks whether the city’s financial resources are translating into the services residents need. From informal settlements and townships to established suburbs, communities across Johannesburg are confronting many of the same challenges: unreliable water supplies, sewage flowing through streets, damaged infrastructure and long-standing maintenance problems. Residents say that even when problems are reported, their complaints often go unanswered. Billions of rands are allocated to municipalities each year for infrastructure and basic services. Yet on the ground, there remains a visible gap between what is budgeted and what communities experience. Cutting Edge examines Johannesburg’s finances, its infrastructure and maintenance backlog, and the challenges facing the city as it tries to keep pace with growing demand. Professor Zondi Mkhabela weighs in on the city’s finances and argues that integrated public-private partnerships may be needed to urgently tackle the infrastructure backlog. He also looks at the impact coalition politics can have on the ability of a city government to deliver services. For residents, these are not simply questions of budgets and political structures. They are daily realities that affect access to water, sanitation, housing and basic dignity. And with voter turnout already low in the previous local government elections, Cutting Edge asks whether growing frustration with service delivery could further influence residents’ willingness to participate in the upcoming polls. videoDescription: Accused number three, Mthobisi Mncube, faced another full day of cross-examination in the Senzo Meyiwa murder trial at the Pretoria High Court on 21 October 2026. Prosecutor Ronnie Sibanda confronted him with what lawyers for the accused, including his own, had earlier told the court about who was with him on the morning of 26 October 2014. Mncube put the difference down to a lawyer’s mistake, saying his co-accused’s advocate “is not a CD” that repeats everything exactly as it was told. The state then turned to the cellphone tower records and the evidence of state witness Sizwe Zungu, who testified that four of the accused were already at the Basotho hostel in Vosloorus when he arrived there that afternoon. Mncube accepts he was in Vosloorus but insists he never went to the hostel. “I hear the lies,” he said of Zungu, adding that a tower picking up his phone does not mean he was at the hostel. When the prosecutor put it to him that his explanation about another man using his phone only came after a later witness testified, Mncube fired back, “If you had not committed any crime…” Sibanda warned him not to accuse him of a crime. Mncube went further, citing the evidence of retired General Vincent Leshabane to allege that witnesses had been pressured to change their statements. videoTitle: The Real Reason Hitler Never Invaded Switzerland
videoDescription: By the summer of 1940, Nazi Germany had crushed Poland, Denmark, Norway, Belgium, the Netherlands, Luxembourg, and France. The swastika flew from the Baltic coast all the way down to the Mediterranean. And yet in the exact middle of occupied Europe, one tiny country of just over four million people remained completely untouched. That country was Switzerland. For six long years of the most destructive war in human history, not one Wehrmacht soldier crossed the Swiss border with a rifle in anger. The real question is why. Hitler despised Switzerland. He called it a pimple on the face of Europe. Goebbels dismissed it as this stinking little state. The Gestapo had already drawn up lists of Swiss politicians, journalists, Jews, and intellectuals to arrest the moment German boots crossed the border. Invasion plans existed. They had code names like Operation Tannenbaum and Fall Grün, division counts, operational timetables, and detailed maps of invasion routes. So what actually stopped him. In this deep dive we unpack the full story. We cover the appointment of General Henri Guisan on August 30, 1939, the famous Rütli speech of July 25, 1940 where Guisan gathered roughly 650 senior officers on a legendary meadow and told them Switzerland would never surrender, and the brilliant Réduit National strategy that would have abandoned the entire Swiss plateau to the invader while locking the Swiss Army into an impregnable Alpine fortress built around Saint-Maurice, Sargans, and the Saint-Gotthard massif. We dig into the thousands of booby-trapped bridges, roads, viaducts, and tunnels that the Swiss Army secretly wired with explosives, including the all-important Gotthard and Simplon railway tunnels that connected Nazi Germany to Fascist Italy. These were the arteries of the Axis war economy, and the Swiss made it clear that if a single German division crossed the border, those arteries would be collapsed into mountains of rubble. But the military deterrent was only one piece of a much darker bargain. We lay out the uncomfortable economic story the Bergier Commission finally forced into public view. We cover the 280 million dollars in Nazi gold the Swiss National Bank purchased from the Reichsbank, including gold looted from occupied central banks and from victims of concentration camps through the SS Melmer accounts. We cover the 84 percent of Swiss munitions exports that went to the Axis powers between 1940 and 1944, the near monopoly on jewel bearings that made Swiss factories indispensable to German bombsights and precision instruments, and the clearing credit system that effectively had Switzerland lending Hitler the money to buy his own weapons. We cover the shadowy role of the Bank for International Settlements in Basel, the darker chapter of refugees turned back in August 1942, and the dramatic final showdown on April 22, 1945, when Italian partisans and Swiss intelligence operatives stopped a Wehrmacht demolition team from dynamiting the Simplon tunnel. The real reason Hitler never invaded Switzerland is not the story we were told in school. It is not luck. It is not just mountains. It is a story about the ruthless mathematics of economic interdependence, the limits of raw military power, and the moral cost of survival in a world on fire. Switzerland made itself militarily too expensive to conquer and economically too valuable to destroy. videoTitle: Konstantin Kisin: France’s Chaos Is Coming for Britain
videoDescription: What began over a month ago as a student protest has devolved into the country’s worst civil unrest in years. On Saturday, hundreds of thousands of demonstrators took to the streets over the rising cost of living and declining public services. Across France, rioters set cars ablaze, looted shops, and attacked municipal buildings. Images of burning streets and ransacked storefronts quickly spread across social media, fueling a debate about what, exactly, is happening to France. Konstantin Kisin, co-host of the Triggernometry podcast and author of An Immigrant’s Love Letter to the West, told me that he thinks France is just the tip of the iceberg. He sees the unrest as the inevitable consequence of decades of mass immigration with little serious effort at integration. Generous social welfare programs subsidized millions of newcomers, demanding nothing in return. Leaders’ dogged embrace of multiculturalism, even as their own citizens increasingly questioned it, ultimately cost the nation its shared identity, the very thing that holds a society together. What Kisin calls the cycle of mutual radicalization—compounded by economic stagnation—explains much of the anger and violence unfolding today. The cultural differences that France and its neighbors so aggressively celebrated could well prove Europe’s undoing. We then turned to Russia and Ukraine. I asked whether the United States bears some responsibility for the war by provoking Russia with the prospect of Ukrainian NATO membership. Kisin was skeptical. It may have influenced the timing or course of the invasion, he said, but it didn’t create the underlying conflict. Russia’s centuries-old drive to expand westward predates NATO. Ukraine has long been caught between two civilizations, and war was always the only way out. I also asked him about Donald Trump’s recent diesel deal with Vladimir Putin, which Kisin thinks has almost nothing to do with ending the war in Ukraine. Kisin sees the deal as an attempt to deflect blame for rising fuel prices ahead of the midterms, even if it means leaving Ukraine virtually indefensible. His larger concern is that Trump's war in Iran has made him desperate for a political victory, and that Ukraine may end up paying the price. videoTitle: Why South Africa Feels Impossible To Fix | South African Economic Crisis | The Blueprint
videoDescription: Why is South Africa, one of the most resource-rich countries in the world, struggling with electricity, unemployment, infrastructure, crime, and economic stagnation? South Africa has enormous reserves of platinum, gold, diamonds and manganese. It has modern cities, major industries, developed financial markets and some of Africa’s most important ports. Yet the country continues to face deep structural challenges. In this episode of The Blueprint, we break down the interconnected problems behind South Africa’s economic crisis, and why fixing them is far more complicated than simply replacing corrupt officials or attracting more investment. We explore: • How Eskom and load shedding became symbols of South Africa’s electricity crisis • Why corruption, ageing infrastructure and political interference weakened the power sector • How problems at Transnet and the freight rail network hurt South Africa’s mining exports • Why cable theft and failing infrastructure make transporting minerals increasingly difficult • How the legacy of Apartheid-era spatial planning still affects access to jobs • Why South Africa continues to struggle with extremely high youth unemployment • How private security, solar power, healthcare and water services created a kind of parallel state • Why skilled-worker emigration and pressure on the tax base create another economic challenge • How ANC politics, cadre deployment, labour unions and coalition government complicate structural reforms • And ultimately, is South Africa really impossible to fix, or does it simply need the political will to make difficult reforms? South Africa’s problems don’t exist independently. Electricity affects mining. Mining depends on railways and ports. Unemployment is connected to education, transport and geography. Weak public services push wealthier citizens toward private alternatives, while political constraints make major reforms difficult. This video explains how all these problems connect, creating a vicious cycle that makes South Africa one of the most fascinating economic and political case studies in the world. videoTitle: DA in knife-edge lead over the ANC in two metros | The Electoral Roadshow with Wayne Sussman
videoDescription: In this edition of the Electoral Road Show with Chris Steyn and analyst Supremo Wayne Sussman, he unpacks the polling results of the first two of six metros surveyed in the highly scientific eNCA MarkData 2026 election poll. In Ekurhuleni, the DA emerged first with 31.2% of the vote, the only party to breach that 30% mark. Second was the ANC with 29.4%. A distant third was MKP at 11.5%. The EFF came in fourth place at 9.2%. In Nelson Mandela Bay, the DA is in the lead with 37.7% of the vote just ahead of the ANC on 37.4%. Coming in third is the EFF at 8%. “The job for the DA as the leading party is how can they stretch that lead in the coming weeks. The job for the ANC is to re-emerge, try to re-emerge as the largest party in Ekurhuleni. And the other parties will be looking at these polls and saying, look, this is a golden opportunity. The ANC is not doing well. What can they extract from the ANC? There's a lot to play for, for each and every single one of the major parties over the next few weeks.” Sussman says questions about service delivery and other key issues produced “very worrying responses for those in government, for those leading. The electorate is not satisfied with the state of local government, with the way our cities are being run.” In next week’s show, the polling results for Johannesburg and Cape Town will be unpacked. videoTitle: Why Prince Mashele Refuses to Give Up on South Africa
videoDescription: He went to school barefoot, without breakfast, and learned to write his name on the ground beneath a tree. Decades later, Prince Mashele became a political analyst, businessman and public intellectual determined to help change South Africa. In this deeply personal conversation between Rob Hersov and Prince Mashele, Mashele opens up about the extraordinary journey from abject poverty in Agincourt to university, government, political analysis and business. He explains how education, relentless reading and a refusal to give up transformed his life and ultimately changed the fortunes of his family. But this interview goes far beyond his personal story. Mashele discusses the historical figures who shaped his understanding of South Africa, including Cecil John Rhodes, Jan Smuts and Nelson Mandela. He explains why he admires each of them for very different reasons, while openly acknowledging the controversies surrounding their legacies. He also reveals how he taught himself English by reading discarded newspapers, why he deliberately limits his public appearances, what he learned from studying leaders such as Charles de Gaulle and Konrad Adenauer, and why he believes humility can lead to greatness. Most importantly, Mashele makes a powerful case for hope. Despite South Africa's enormous challenges, he believes the country can still become a great nation potentially a Switzerland or Singapore of Africa if people are prepared to contribute to its future. This is the story behind the political analyst: the poverty, the education, the books, the ambition, the historical perspective and the determination to never stop. Watch the full conversation and discover the man behind the political commentary. videoDescription: South Africa is approaching another important political moment — but what is really happening beneath the headlines? In this episode of the King David Studio Podcast, David Mashabela sits down with political analyst Sandile Swana for a wide-ranging conversation about South Africa’s changing political landscape. The discussion looks beyond political party slogans and personalities to examine the deeper questions facing the country: the changing position of the ANC, the rise of alternative political formations, coalition government, political violence, local government, corruption, state institutions and the growing battle for control of South Africa’s municipalities. With the 2026 Local Government Elections scheduled for 4 November, political parties are competing for control of councils and metros in a landscape that has become increasingly fragmented. Swana has also raised concerns publicly about politically linked killings around municipal politics and has argued that competition for political office can intersect with control over municipal resources and procurement. These remain his analysis and interpretation rather than established findings about every incident. The conversation also examines the Madlanga Commission, the questions it has raised about South Africa’s criminal justice system and what accountability could mean for public confidence in state institutions. The Commission was established following allegations made by KwaZulu-Natal Police Commissioner Lt-Gen Nhlanhla Mkhwanazi and continues its work, with its final report now due in January 2027. David and Sandile explore some of the bigger questions: Is South Africa moving permanently into an era of coalition government? Can the ANC reverse its electoral losses? What explains the intensity of competition for municipal political positions? Why have political killings remained a concern around local politics? Are South Africa’s institutions strong enough to withstand political interference? What could the 2026 local elections tell us about the country's longer-term political direction? This is not simply a conversation about who wins the next election. It is a discussion about power, governance, accountability and the future of South Africa’s democracy.
